hero.title: Subtitling Services for eLearning & Video Localization
hero.lead: Subtitle preparation, timed-text production and media-localization support for localization service providers, training-content teams and digital publishers.
paragraphs: Timed subtitle and caption-file preparation for eligible video and learning media, based on approved scripts, languages and delivery specifications.

lead.text: The source video, approved language content and technical delivery rules determine how the subtitle file should be prepared.
Different projects may require different timing conventions, reading-speed limits, line lengths, positioning instructions and output formats.
EPUBTRANS supports subtitling production as an individual assignment or as a separately scoped part of a localization or eLearning project.

blocks.text: Subtitle text needs to appear in a way that corresponds with the relevant audio and visual content.
Depending on the project, timing work may involve identifying the beginning and end of spoken segments, preparing timecodes and reviewing the relationship between subtitle cues and the media.
The required timing precision and acceptable conventions should be supplied or agreed before work begins.
Different receiving systems may have their own timing restrictions.
Subtitle production involves dividing speech into readable units.
Appropriate segmentation can depend on sentence structure, the available screen time, reading requirements and the target language.
Work may include reviewing line breaks, balancing subtitle length and avoiding unnecessary fragmentation of meaning.
Subtitle presentation should reflect the agreed specification rather than a universal character or reading-speed rule.
A subtitle file may need particular text conventions, punctuation, line lengths or styling instructions.
Depending on the required output, the work can involve preparing the subtitle text and timecodes in the agreed file structure.
The appearance of the final subtitles may also depend on the media player, authoring tool or video distribution environment.
Not every subtitle file format supports the same styling or positioning features.
Some clients already have subtitle files that require revision.
The requested work may involve updating approved text, correcting timing, adjusting segmentation or adapting the file to another specified output.
Where translated subtitles are supplied, the task may be limited to production-level corrections rather than full linguistic review.
The distinction should be clear in the project brief.
A video may require subtitle tracks in several languages.
EPUBTRANS can assess multilingual subtitle production using the agreed target-language content, source media and delivery rules.
The scope should identify whether EPUBTRANS is working from client-approved translations or whether translation and linguistic review must also be separately commissioned.
Language availability, specialist subject requirements and reviewer responsibilities must be confirmed for each project.

sections.title: Working with Translation Agencies and LSPs

lead.text: EPUBTRANS prepares agreed subtitle assets from supplied media, scripts and approved translations; the commissioning LSP retains translation management, terminology, linguistic review and client approval unless a different responsibility is agreed.

blocks.text: Where translated scripts are already approved, subtitling production can focus on their representation as timed text.
If the translated wording is too long for the available screen time, a linguistic decision may be needed.
Production staff should flag such issues rather than independently changing approved meaning without authorization.
Some languages require particular care with font support, script rendering, text direction and line-breaking conventions.
These requirements should be reviewed against the source media, subtitle format and intended delivery environment.
Current support for specific languages, scripts and platforms requires confirmation before committing to the project.

lead.text: Subtitles and captions can use similar technical methods, but their intended purpose may differ.

blocks.text: Translated subtitles commonly convey spoken dialogue or narration in another language.
They are typically designed for viewers who can hear the audio but need the speech represented in a language they understand.
Captions may provide a synchronized text alternative to speech and meaningful nonspeech audio information.
Depending on the content, this can include speaker identification, important sounds and other audio cues needed for comprehension.

groups.title: Subtitles for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Audiences

blocks.text: Some projects specify subtitles for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, commonly referred to as SDH.
These may require additional conventions beyond translation-only subtitles, including suitable treatment of speakers and meaningful sounds.
A translated subtitle file is not automatically equivalent to an accessibility-compliant caption track.
The applicable accessibility requirements, editorial conventions, target platform and acceptance criteria must be identified.

EPUBTRANS can assess supported caption-related production requirements, but compliance with WCAG or another accessibility standard must not be claimed unless the relevant checks are actually performed and the complete media experience is evaluated.

lead.text: Subtitle and caption files may be delivered separately from the video or integrated into another production workflow.
The correct approach depends on the receiving platform.

blocks.text: Common timed-text formats include SubRip Subtitle (SRT) and Web Video Text Tracks (WebVTT).
Other workflows may involve specialized subtitle or caption formats with additional technical requirements.
These are examples of formats used in the industry, not a claim that EPUBTRANS currently supports every format or platform implementation.
Please identify the required extension, specification and destination when requesting a quote.
A project may require standalone subtitle tracks to be imported into a video platform, eLearning authoring tool or multimedia player.
The delivery agreement should define the languages, file naming, text encoding, timecode conventions and any relevant compatibility requirements.
Some projects require subtitles to be permanently displayed within the video image.
This involves video-processing considerations beyond delivering a standalone subtitle file and must be separately assessed.
A file that is technically valid in one subtitle format may not meet the requirements of every learning platform, video player or distribution service.
Platform-specific conversion, rendering tests and final upload or integration are separate work items unless explicitly included.
Learning materials may include instructional videos, demonstrations, screen recordings and narrated presentations.
Subtitle work can be coordinated with course localization, but the interaction between video tracks, authoring-tool files and published learning packages must be defined for each project.
Rebuilding an eLearning course, integrating subtitles into a native authoring file and testing an LMS package are not automatically included in standalone subtitling.
Publishers and educational organizations may need subtitles for lectures, seminars, author interviews, instructional recordings and digital-learning resources.
Specialist terminology, names, equations and references to visual content may require approved source materials or subject-matter clarification.
Business training, onboarding, demonstrations and presentations may require timed-text outputs for different markets.
The target languages, brand terminology, approved scripts and intended publication environment help determine the appropriate production method.
Recorded webinars can involve multiple speakers, technical terminology and inconsistent audio quality.
A subtitle assignment may require transcription or a corrected source script before timing can begin.
That preparatory work should be identified in the quotation.

lead.text: A representative media sample helps establish a realistic production scope.

blocks.text: Depending on the assignment, useful inputs include:

items: Video duration and approximate number of assets
Source language and required target languages
Approved source transcripts or scripts, where available
Translated scripts or subtitle text, where available
Intended video platform or eLearning authoring environment
Instructions for relevant sound cues or speaker labels
Preferred schedule and final delivery method

blocks.text: Not every item applies to every project.
Clear audio and complete scripts generally make subtitle preparation more straightforward than recordings containing noise, overlapping speech or missing source information.
Where translated text has not been supplied, the translation requirement must be assessed separately.
Where the source video is incomplete or changing, subtitle timing may need to be revised after the final video is approved.

lead.text: The agreed deliverables depend on the work requested.

items: Updated subtitle files based on client feedback
Timed-text files in an agreed supported format
A subtitle issue list or query report where commissioned
Supporting file lists or delivery notes

lead.text: The output specification should identify the required languages, file formats, timecodes and review expectations.
Translated scripts, video exports, embedded subtitles, accessibility reports and integration into an eLearning or video platform are not automatically part of every subtitle-production assignment.

blocks.text: We examine the representative source files, available scripts, target languages and intended delivery format.
The review identifies any transcription, translation, timing or platform-specific dependencies.
We agree which services are included and who is responsible for the supplied language content, linguistic review, subtitle timing, caption cues and final platform acceptance.
Delivery formats, file naming, review cycles and acceptance criteria are also defined.
The agreed text is organized and timed according to the project instructions.
Any source inconsistencies or language issues requiring authorization are recorded for client review.
Checks may cover synchronization, segmentation, text consistency, timecode structure, required conventions and compatibility where the relevant tools and media are available.
Linguistic and accessibility-specific review activities are included only when commissioned.
Completed subtitle files and any required supporting information are prepared for the specified handoff.
Changes to approved translations, revised source videos and further correction rounds are handled according to the project agreement.

lead.text: Useful subtitle files need to represent the approved content in a readable, synchronized form.

Depending on the agreed scope, production quality checks may include timing and cue order, line breaks, punctuation, missing text, duplicate segments, file naming and correct identification of the target language.

blocks.text: Where included, the delivered subtitle files may be reviewed alongside the supplied media to identify obvious timing or display issues.
Full platform-specific integration testing must be explicitly agreed.
Subtitle timing and technical QA should not be confused with independent verification of the translated content.
The client or designated linguistic reviewer is responsible for approving translation choices unless linguistic review is separately included.
Captioning for accessibility may require inclusion of meaningful nonspeech audio, speaker identification and other conventions.
The applicable review standard should be agreed before production.
The client should confirm authorization to provide media, scripts and related materials.
Unreleased training, educational or business recordings may require particular handling instructions and an approved transfer method.
EPUBTRANS does not guarantee error-free output, universal platform compatibility or accessibility conformance without defined scope and appropriate evidence.

sections.title: What Affects Subtitling Scope and Scheduling?

blocks.text: Long recordings, background noise, overlapping speakers and unclear dialogue can require additional preparation.
Additional target languages increase the number of subtitle tracks and language-specific requirements.
Existing transcripts and translations may reduce the amount of preparatory work, provided they match the final media.
Detailed segmentation rules, caption requirements and destination-specific formatting can change the production effort.
Changes to the source video, scripts or translations after timing may require rework.
Translation, linguistic review, transcription, accessibility captioning, video processing and eLearning integration may need separately agreed tasks and reviewers.
These requirements should be reviewed before estimates or schedules are confirmed.

Converting supplied audio or video speech into readable text, with timestamps and formatting where commissioned.
Production support for localized course content, related media assets and supported eLearning authoring workflows.
A broader overview of EPUBTRANS's production support for LSPs and translation agencies.
Document layout and formatting for multilingual publishing and localized content.
Accessibility-related production for supported digital content, documents and publishing formats.

groups.title: What does EPUBTRANS's subtitling service include?

blocks.text: EPUBTRANS's documented media-production scope includes subtitle and timed-text activities. Depending on the brief, a project may involve synchronization, segmentation, formatting or corrections to approved subtitle content.

groups.title: Can you work with translations supplied by our localization agency?

blocks.text: Client-approved translations can be used as source assets for a subtitling project. The required language, formatting rules and responsibility for linguistic review should be confirmed.
Not automatically. Translation may be commissioned separately or supplied by the client. The project brief should identify who produces and approves the target-language text.

groups.title: What is the difference between subtitles and captions?

blocks.text: Translated subtitles commonly convey speech in another language. Captions can include same-language speech and meaningful nonspeech audio information, such as important sounds and speaker identification.

groups.title: Do you provide SRT and VTT subtitle files?

blocks.text: SRT and VTT are common timed-text formats. Current output-format and feature support must be confirmed against the project's technical requirements.

groups.title: Can you synchronize existing subtitles with a video?

blocks.text: Existing subtitle timing and synchronization work can be assessed using the supplied media and files. The scope should identify whether text corrections or complete retiming are needed.

groups.title: Can you prepare multilingual subtitles for eLearning courses?

blocks.text: Multilingual subtitle preparation can be assessed using approved language content and source media. Integration into Storyline, Rise, Lectora or another authoring environment is a separate requirement unless included in the project.

groups.title: Do you provide captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers?

blocks.text: Caption-related production can be assessed where the applicable conventions, media and requirements are supplied. The exact accessibility checks and deliverables require agreement.

groups.title: Can you add subtitles directly into our final video?

blocks.text: Embedding or burning subtitles into a video requires separate video-processing work. Please identify the source video format and required final output so feasibility can be confirmed.
Language and script availability depend on the project, source assets and required linguistic or technical work. Please specify the target locales and requirements for assessment.

groups.title: Can you guarantee that subtitles comply with accessibility standards?

blocks.text: No. Accessibility conformance depends on the applicable requirements and the completed media experience. Specific caption-production and validation tasks must be agreed and supported by evidence.

groups.title: What information is needed for a subtitling quote?

blocks.text: Please provide a sample video, duration, source and target languages, available transcripts or translations, output format, target platform, timing requirements and preferred schedule.

lead.text: Need timed subtitles for a video, training course or multilingual media project?
Share your source media, target languages, approved text assets and intended delivery format with EPUBTRANS.
We can review the requirements and discuss the subtitling production, quality checks and related services appropriate to your project.
